questions.stem: Represent the relation $x + 2y + 2 = 0$ graphically by dragging two points. Find the slope and the length of the part of the y-axis between the origin and the line.

pending_review.why: It needs the correct slope -1/2 with a wrong intercept. A student who reads coefficients without isolating y gets the slope wrong too (m=1), so they would not fire it. Correct-slope, wrong-intercept lines come from other slips, such as a sign error on c or forgetting to divide by 2. / This fires when the slope is -1/2 but the intercept is wrong. A student who got -1/2 must have isolated y, so she would normally have the intercept right too. A wrong intercept there is more likely a sign or arithmetic slip, such as b=+1. Reading coefficients without isolating y gives a wrong slope, so this predicate mostly fires for other reasons.

canonical_solution.text_md: Isolate $y$: $2y = -x - 2$, so $y = -\frac{1}{2}x - 1$.
The slope is $m = -\frac{1}{2}$.
The line crosses the y-axis at (0, -1), so the length is 1.
Plot (0, -1) and (2, -2), then draw the line through them.

questions.stem: Represent the relation $x - 2y + 4 = 0$ graphically by dragging two points. Then read the slope of the line and the length of the part of the y-axis between the origin and the line.

pending_review.why: Fires on slope 1/2 with an intercept other than 2. A student who reads coefficients off the unisolated equation takes m=1 here (the x coefficient), so the slope is wrong too. That case lands in off-target, not here. Slope 1/2 with b=4 is not what this misconception produces, so the diagnosis would mostly fire for another error, such as an arithmetic slip in the intercept. / This needs slope 0.5 with an intercept other than 2. A student who reads the constant straight off without isolating y also gets the slope wrong, because the x coefficient is 1, not 1/2. A correct slope with a wrong intercept would mostly come from an arithmetic slip, not from this misconception. Attributing it to this misconception would be wrong.

canonical_solution.text_md: Isolate $y$: $2y = x + 4$, so $y = \frac{1}{2}x + 2$.
The slope is $m = \frac{1}{2}$ (also $-\frac{a}{b} = -\frac{1}{-2}$).
The y-intercept is $b = 2$: the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 2), so the length is 2.
Plot (0, 2), then go 2 right and 1 up to get (2, 3), and draw the line through them.

questions.stem: Represent the relation $2x + y - 3 = 0$ graphically by dragging two points. State the slope and the length of the y-intercept.

pending_review.why: Fires on slope -2 with an intercept other than 3, a parallel line. A student who reads coefficients without isolating y takes slope 2 (not -2) and intercept -3, so this error would not produce a correct slope. The predicate fires for other slips, such as arithmetic errors. / Fires on slope -2 with an intercept other than 3. A student who reads coefficients straight off 2x + y - 3 = 0 gets slope +2 (not -2), so they would not keep the correct slope; this construction would come from a different error.

Fires when neither slope nor intercept matches and the slope is not a plain sign flip. The coefficient-reading student's line (m=2, b=-3) has slope magnitude 2 with the sign flipped, so it would most likely be caught by slope-sign-flipped first. Off-target is a catch-all with no specific link to this misconception.

canonical_solution.text_md: Isolate $y$: $y = -2x + 3$.
The slope is $m = -2$, and $-\frac{a}{b} = -\frac{2}{1} = -2$ agrees.
The y-intercept is $b = 3$, so the line passes through (0, 3).
Plot (0, 3) and (1, 1), then draw the line through them.

questions.stem: For the function $n(x)=\frac{x-1}{x^2-9}$, mark every value of $x$ that must be excluded from the domain.

pending_review.why: A student who excludes numerator zeroes would mark x=1 instead of ±3, so the marks would be {1}. That does fire extra-values, because 1 is not in the answer set. But it would also fire missed-values, and extra-values fires on any stray mark, such as a sign error or a guessed value. It is not specific to this misconception, so the diagnosis is not safe.

canonical_solution.text_md: Only the denominator can make the fraction undefined, so solve $x^2-9=0$.
Mark $-3$ and $3$; the domain is $R-\{-3,3\}$.
$x=1$ makes the numerator zero, so $n(1)=0$ is defined and 1 stays in the domain.

questions.stem: For the function $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-4}$, mark on the number line every value of $x$ that is NOT in the domain.

pending_review.why: It fires when only part of the set is marked, for example just 2, or just -2. A student holding the one-root-only-denominator misconception would mark only the positive root, 2, and that does trigger missed-values. But missed-values also fires for any partial answer, such as marking only -2, or marking one root plus a stray value. It is a generic partial-set signal, so it is not specific to this misconception. The 'when in doubt, false' rule applies.

It fires when the student marks values outside the answer set. A student who sets the numerator to zero marks x=-1, and -1 is an extra value, so the predicate would fire. But that student would also leave out -2 and 2, so the construction is only a partial match for the excludes-numerator-zeroes error. The predicate would also fire for many other errors, such as marking 4 or 0. It is not specific to this misconception.

canonical_solution.text_md: The domain is R minus the zeroes of the denominator, so set the denominator equal to zero: $x^2-4=0$.
Then $x^2=4$, so $x=2$ or $x=-2$ (a square has two roots).
Mark both $-2$ and $2$; the domain is $R-\{-2,2\}$.
The numerator's zero ($x=-1$) does not matter for the domain.

misconceptions.label: Reading m and b straight off the equation without isolating y
misconceptions.description: The student takes the number in front of $x$ as the slope, or the constant term as the y-intercept, without first writing the equation as $y = mx + b$.

misconceptions.label: Slope written as a/b, losing the minus
misconceptions.description: The student uses the slope rule on $ax + by + c = 0$ but writes $m = \frac{a}{b}$ instead of $-\frac{a}{b}$.

misconceptions.label: Finds only the positive root of the denominator
misconceptions.description: When the denominator has the form $x^2=k$, the student gives only $x=\sqrt{k}$ and loses the negative root.
